prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses.  Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups

- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

- Accessibility
Safety

Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Landscape-recreation roads Definition: roads with prominent landscape features, along which parks, green spaces, and recreational facilities are distributed. Design focus: create road scenes with smooth slow-mobility circulation, beautiful scenery, openness and transparency, and convenient facilities. Historic-style streets and lanes Definition: streets and lanes that preserve abundant cultural relics, concentrate historic buildings, can more completely reflect the traditional spatial pattern, and have a certain scale. Design focus: prioritize slow mobility, continue the historic and cultural character, and enhance vitality and activity. Smart-city demonstration roads Definition: roads that, through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, achieve deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, and serve as a showcase and promotion of Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. Design focus: based on an integrated framework of the traffic-participant subsystem, roadside subsystem, and central subsystem. Emphasis is placed on “the road” and “the cloud,” providing intelligent services for “vehicles” and “people.” Comprehensive roads Definition: roads with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and with characteristics of two or more road types. Design focus: carry out targeted road design according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. 7 Road-type functional traffic corridors Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • The design should respond to the needs of different traffic modes, including motor vehicles, non-motorized traffic, public transport, freight transport, and pedestrian traffic, with a coordinated allocation of space. • At intersections where signal lights are installed, allow motor vehicles to pass with longer distances and higher speeds as much as possible, reducing crossings by motor vehicles and pedestrians.
